title: The Two Worlds of the Red Shirt: from the Lagoa dos Patos to the Volturno
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Nice, Quai Papacino: birth on the old port
stops.date_confidence: attested. Italian Wikipedia gives the birthplace as Quai Papacino on the old port; the coordinate is that quay. An English-language dossier reading of Rue de la Providence, about 450 metres west in the Vieux-Nice street grid, is not carried here.
stops.campa: In the old port quarter of Nice, on the Quai Papacino, a third child is born to the coasting trader Domenico Garibaldi and Rosa Raimondi, and named Giuseppe Maria. The city belongs this year to the French Empire; in seven years it will belong again to the Kingdom of Sardinia, so the boy grows up the subject of a crown he will one day hand a kingdom to and never serve. His father works the Ligurian coast in small craft, carrying wine and salt. Giuseppe is put to that trade as a boy, and to no other.
stops.quote: To the piety of my mother, to her beneficent and charitable nature, do I not, perhaps, owe that little love of country which has gained for me the sympathy and affection of my good, but unfortunate fellow-citizens?
stops.quote_source: Giuseppe Garibaldi, The Life of General Garibaldi, Written by Himself, trans. Theodore Dwight (New York, 1859)
suggested_refs: The traditional birth house on the Quai Papacino, Nice, on the quay of the old port
sources: Garibaldi, The Life of General Garibaldi, trans. Dwight (1859), Project Gutenberg 50544

stops.name: Pera, Constantinople: the unlit years
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the residence and the teaching; the dates are loose, given in sources as roughly 1828 to 1832, and the month is a placeholder. Every reachable source is thin on why he stayed.
stops.campa: The young merchant sailor is held in the Ottoman capital by war and quarantine, and stays. In the European quarter across the Golden Horn he teaches Italian, French, and mathematics in the households of the Pera merchants, a man of twenty-one with no politics yet and no country worth the word. Biographies pass over these years quickly because the documents run out. Four years of a life otherwise recorded almost daily are missing here. He never explained them.
suggested_refs: The Pera quarter of Constantinople, across the Golden Horn from the old city

stops.name: Taganrog, the Sea of Azov: news of Young Italy
stops.date_confidence: attested for April 1833 and the voyage of the Clorinda; the day is a placeholder. The exile who gave him the news is traditionally identified as Giovanni Battista Cuneo, an identification old and widely repeated but not pinned to a document.
stops.campa: Aboard the schooner Clorinda, working up the Sea of Azov toward the Russian grain port, Garibaldi falls into conversation with an Italian exile who tells him there is a movement, that it has a name, Young Italy, and that Italy is a thing that could be made. He is twenty-five and has never heard the argument put whole. He goes ashore at Taganrog a conspirator. Grain is loaded for the run home. Whether the exile who talked to him was Giovanni Battista Cuneo, as the tradition has it, no document says.
stops.quote: Surely Columbus did not enjoy so much satisfaction on the discovery of America, as I experienced on hearing that the redemption of our country was meditated.
stops.quote_source: Giuseppe Garibaldi, The Life of General Garibaldi, trans. Theodore Dwight (New York, 1859)
suggested_refs: The Russian grain port of Taganrog on the Sea of Azov, terminus of the Clorinda's voyage
sources: Garibaldi, The Life of General Garibaldi, trans. Dwight (1859), Project Gutenberg 50544

stops.name: Genoa, the oath and the war name
stops.date_confidence: [R] tradition, and contested. English-language sources place a meeting with Mazzini at Genoa in November 1833; Italian Wikipedia states the date and place are uncertain, gives Marseille as the alleged site, and notes Mazzini had left for Geneva by June 1833 and was not in Genoa that November. The enrolment in Young Italy in this period is secure; the meeting is not. Day is a placeholder.
stops.campa: Genoa, the winter of the conspiracy. Garibaldi comes to the man whose movement he first heard named in a Russian port, and takes from Giuseppe Mazzini the oath of Young Italy and a war name out of Plutarch, Cleombroto. From here the sailor is an agent. The plan is a rising in Genoa timed to a Savoyard incursion out of Switzerland, and his part in it is to carry the crews of the Royal Sardinian Navy over from inside. He enlists in that navy in order to subvert it. He is twenty-six years old.
suggested_refs: The Young Italy oath of enrolment, taken under the conspiratorial name Cleombroto

stops.name: Genoa, the gate of the Lanterna
stops.date_confidence: attested; the date and hour of the escape are Garibaldi's own, given in his autobiography. The death sentence handed down in absentia by a Genoese military tribunal that year is documented.
stops.campa: The rising does not happen. The Savoyard column dissolves in the passes, the fleet does not turn, the arrests begin, and on the evening of the fifth of February Garibaldi walks out through the gate of the Lanterna dressed as a peasant and keeps walking. He is in Marseille four days later. In June a Genoese tribunal condemns him to death in his absence as an enemy of the state, and prints the sentence in the newspapers. That printing is the first time he sees his own name in a paper.
stops.quote: At that time my public life commenced; and, a few days after, I saw my name, for the first time, in a newspaper: but it was in a sentence of death!
stops.quote_source: Giuseppe Garibaldi, The Life of General Garibaldi, trans. Theodore Dwight (New York, 1859)
suggested_refs: The Porta della Lanterna, Genoa, gate of the flight of 5 February 1834
sources: Garibaldi, The Life of General Garibaldi, trans. Dwight (1859), Project Gutenberg 50544

stops.name: Rio Grande do Sul, the boats carried overland
stops.date_confidence: attested for the service with the Riograndense Republic from 1835; the month and day are placeholders and the coordinate is the provincial pin at Porto Alegre, not a single camp.
stops.campa: Under letters of marque from a republic a few months old, Garibaldi fits out small craft on the Lagoa dos Patos and raids imperial Brazilian shipping for the Ragamuffins of Rio Grande do Sul. When the lagoon is closed to him he has the boats hauled out of the water and dragged overland on ox carts to the open Atlantic, then put back into the sea on the far side. He is twenty-eight. The whole navy of the Riograndense Republic is what he can drag across a sandbar on an ox cart.
suggested_refs: The Lagoa dos Patos and the overland portage of the Riograndense flotilla

stops.name: Gualeguay, Entre Rios: the prisoner
stops.date_confidence: [R]. The imprisonment and the torture are widely repeated and reach us chiefly through Garibaldi's own memoirs; the Wikipedia article on Gualeguay does not mention him at all, and this pass found no independent confirmation. Coordinate corrected to the town itself; month and day are placeholders.
stops.campa: Taken in Argentine waters and carried inland to Gualeguay on the river bank, Garibaldi is held some months by a government that does not recognise a rebel commission and sees only a pirate. The accounts descending from him tell of an attempted escape, a recapture, and a strappado, hung by the wrists from a beam until he lost consciousness. He gets out, crosses back to the Brazilian war, and is at sea again inside the year. He is thirty. No source outside his own memoirs records that he was ever in Gualeguay at all.
suggested_refs: The town of Gualeguay, Entre Rios, on the Gualeguay river
sources: Dossier lead from Garibaldi's memoirs, not independently confirmed

stops.name: Imbituba, the flotilla off Santa Catarina
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1839 and the Imbituba action; month and day are placeholders, the engagement falling in the Juliana campaign of that year.
stops.campa: The Riograndense flotilla stands in to the Santa Catarina coast to raise a second republic, the Juliana, and fights an action off Imbituba against imperial vessels with the odds and the weather both against it. Garibaldi commands from a deck he has fitted out himself, with crews drawn off the fishing beaches of the shore. The Juliana Republic will last four months. He is by now a naval officer of two rebel states that no government on earth has recognised. He is thirty-two.
suggested_refs: The Juliana Republic of Santa Catarina, proclaimed and extinguished in 1839

stops.name: Laguna, the woman on the shore
stops.date_confidence: attested for the meeting at Laguna in October 1839 after the rebel recapture of the town; day is a placeholder. The telescope sighting and the words carried in the quote field are memoir tradition, not documented dialogue.
stops.campa: The rebels retake Laguna and Garibaldi comes ashore into the town. He sees Ana Maria de Jesus Ribeiro, called Anita, nineteen, married four years to a shoemaker of the place, and within days she is aboard the Rio Pardo and will not leave it. She rides, shoots, and handles a boat as well as any man in the flotilla. From this month she is with him in every campaign he fights for the next ten years, in Brazil, in Uruguay, and in Italy. What he said to her on the shore that day comes down only through his own memoirs.
stops.quote_source: Traditional, from Garibaldi's retrospective memoirs, on first seeing Anita at Laguna, 1839
suggested_refs: The waterfront of Laguna, Santa Catarina, retaken by the rebels in October 1839

stops.name: Montevideo, the church of St Francis of Assisi
stops.date_confidence: attested for the marriage on 26 March 1842 in the old town. The legal standing of Anita's first marriage, and whether her first husband was in fact dead, remain disputed among biographers.
stops.campa: Two years in Montevideo as a trader and a schoolmaster teaching mathematics have not made a civilian of him. In the church of St Francis of Assisi in the old town Garibaldi marries Anita, the pair having declared her first husband dead. Whether he was dead, and whether that first marriage was ever dissolved, biographers still argue over. Their son Menotti is nearly two, born in a Brazilian camp during a retreat; his mother carried him out of it slung at her neck in a scarf.
suggested_refs: The Iglesia de San Francisco de Asis in the Ciudad Vieja of Montevideo

stops.name: Costa Brava, the Parana: the ships burned
stops.date_confidence: [R] for the detail. The action of August 1842 is standard biography but was not independently reconfirmed this pass; the coordinate approximates the river reach rather than a pinned site, and the day is a placeholder.
stops.campa: Rosas sends Admiral William Brown's Argentine squadron up the Parana after the small Uruguayan flotilla Garibaldi commands, and catches it. Outgunned and shot away, Garibaldi fights the day out, then takes off his crews and burns his own vessels to the waterline so Brown will have nothing to tow home. He walks out of the river country with what is left of his men and no ships at all. The blockade of Montevideo has another eight years to run. This is the only time Garibaldi and the Rosas regime meet each other directly under arms.
suggested_refs: The Costa Brava reach of the Parana, and Admiral William Brown's Argentine squadron

stops.name: Montevideo, the Italian Legion in red
stops.date_confidence: attested. Italian Wikipedia dates the founding of the Legione Italiana, with its red uniforms, to the end of 1843; the command of the Uruguayan fleet in 1842 is a separate and earlier appointment. The day is a placeholder.
stops.campa: For the defence of a city besieged from the Cerrito by Oribe's army, Garibaldi raises a legion out of the Italian exiles of Montevideo and clothes it in red. The story told ever after is that the shirts were slaughterhouse stock, cut for the workers of the saladeros and unsellable since the Rio Grande markets closed, bought up cheap by a quartermaster with no money. Red does not show blood. He puts one on himself that winter and wears the colour for the rest of his life. No invoice survives to say where the cloth came from.
suggested_refs: The Legione Italiana of Montevideo, founded late 1843; the saladero shirts of the Rio de la Plata

stops.name: San Antonio del Salto, the two hundred
stops.date_confidence: attested for 8 February 1846 at the Don Venancio saladero on the San Antonio stream near Salto. The engagement is the Batalla de San Antonio; the string Battle of San Antonio del Santo, current in English sources, corresponds to no real place name.
stops.campa: At a saladero on the San Antonio stream near Salto, fewer than two hundred Italian legionaries and about a hundred cavalry are surrounded by more than a thousand of Servando Gomez's horse and two hundred infantry. Garibaldi puts his men inside the slaughterhouse walls and holds through the day, then breaks out in the dark with his wounded and reaches Salto. Montevideo orders his name read at the head of the army list. The exile press in Italy prints the story and prints it again. Nobody in Turin has met him.
suggested_refs: The Don Venancio saladero on the arroyo San Antonio, near Salto, Uruguay

stops.name: Montevideo, the Speranza sails
stops.date_confidence: attested. The Palermo rising of 12 January 1848 is the news, not the departure: Garibaldi sailed from Montevideo on 15 April 1848 and reached Nice on 21 June. The ship bought by subscription of the Italian community is named as the Speranza in standard biography, not reconfirmed from a fetched source this pass.
stops.campa: News of the Palermo rising of January crosses the Atlantic and reaches the Rio de la Plata in the southern autumn. The Italians of Montevideo buy a ship by subscription and name her Speranza, and Garibaldi sails on the fifteenth of April with some sixty legionaries and his family aboard. He raises Nice on the twenty-first of June, fourteen years after a Genoese court sentenced him to death. He is said to have written to the new Pope offering the legion's sword for the liberation of Italy; no answer to that letter is recorded.
suggested_refs: The Speranza, bought by subscription among the Italians of Montevideo in 1848
sources: Dossier lead on the ship's name, not independently reconfirmed

segments.name: Rome, and the Republic That Fell

stops.name: The Janiculum, Rome: Oudinot turned back
stops.date_confidence: attested for 30 April 1849 at the Janiculum wall and the French repulse, and for the siege proper opening on 1 June.
stops.campa: The Republic proclaimed in February holds Rome, and France sends Oudinot to put the Pope back into it. On the thirtieth of April the French come at the Janiculum wall by the Villa Corsini, and Garibaldi's volunteers, students, exiles, and legionaries brought from Montevideo, throw them back down the slope with the bayonet and take prisoners by the hundred. He asks leave to pursue them to the sea and Mazzini's government refuses him, being still in negotiation. The siege proper opens on the first of June.
suggested_refs: The Villa Corsini and the Janiculum wall, ground of the fighting of 30 April 1849

stops.name: Rome, the Assembly on the last day
stops.date_confidence: attested for 30 June 1849 and for the canonical wording carried in the quote field. The coordinate is the city pin: the hall in which the Assembly sat is not specified in the sources consulted, so no landmark point is claimed.
stops.campa: The wall is breached, the Villa Spada position gone, the volunteers cut up on the Janiculum, and the Assembly resolves that resistance is no longer possible. Garibaldi comes into the chamber straight off the line, dust and blood dried into his shirt, the sabre bent in its scabbard, and tells the deputies he is leaving Rome and going on with whoever will follow him. The vote is taken the same day. The French will enter the city on the third of July and restore the Pope's temporal power.
stops.quote_source: Garibaldi to the Roman Assembly, 30 June 1849
suggested_refs: The last session of the Assembly of the Roman Republic, 30 June 1849

stops.name: Saint Peter's Square, the offer
stops.date_confidence: attested for the address in Saint Peter's Square on 2 July 1849 and for the withdrawal of about four thousand men. The wording in the quote field is [R]: it comes through Trevelyan's Defence of the Roman Republic (1907) as cited on Wikiquote, and was not verified in the primary edition. It is a separate speech from the one of 30 June and is not to be merged with it.
stops.campa: Two days after the Assembly's last vote, with the French entering the city tomorrow, Garibaldi puts his horse in front of the men still under arms in the square before Saint Peter's and tells them precisely what he has to offer, which is nothing. Four thousand go with him that afternoon, out through the Porta San Giovanni toward Venice, across a peninsula held by Austrian, French, Spanish, Neapolitan, and papal troops at once. Anita rides out with the column, pregnant with their fifth child.
stops.quote: I offer neither pay, nor quarters, nor provisions; I offer hunger, thirst, forced marches, battles and death. Let him who loves his country in his heart, and not with his lips only, follow me.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Garibaldi in Saint Peter's Square, 2 July 1849, via G. M. Trevelyan, Garibaldi's Defence of the Roman Republic (1907)
suggested_refs: The march out of Rome by the Porta San Giovanni, 2 July 1849

stops.name: Guiccioli farm, Mandriole: Anita
stops.date_confidence: attested for 4 August 1849 at 7:45 pm at the Guiccioli farm at Mandriole, near Ravenna. English-language sources give the looser near Comacchio, which is the landing point from the Adriatic, some twenty-five kilometres north.
stops.campa: The column has dissolved. Austrian patrols are working the Comacchio lagoon and the fishing boats that carried the last of them up the Adriatic have been taken or scattered. Garibaldi carries Anita ashore and inland to a farm at Mandriole outside Ravenna, where a doctor is sent for and arrives too late. She dies at a quarter to eight in the evening, malarial, worn out, and five months pregnant. He is hunted across the Romagna for weeks after, moved farmhouse to farmhouse by men whose names he is not told.
suggested_refs: The Guiccioli farm at Mandriole, near Ravenna; her body reinterred several times and finally on the Janiculum in 1932

stops.name: Tangier, the winter of the memoirs
stops.date_confidence: attested for the flight to Tangier in 1849 under Piedmontese pressure to leave; the month and day are placeholders. Coordinate inherited from the canonical Tangier pin already in use in the atlas.
stops.campa: Piedmont picks him up on the Ligurian coast, holds him, and makes it plain that a Garibaldi at large in Italy is a difficulty the crown would rather export. He takes ship for Morocco and passes the winter at Tangier in the house of the Sardinian consul, writing the first draft of his memoirs. He is forty-two, with no wife, no country, no command, and no plan. His surviving children are in Nice with his mother. One Italian state has condemned him to death and another has now put him out.
suggested_refs: The house of the Sardinian consul at Tangier, where the first draft of the memoirs was written

stops.name: Staten Island, the candle factory
stops.date_confidence: attested for the arrival at New York on 30 July 1850 and for the employment with Meucci at Rosebank. Coordinate inherited from the Rosebank pin already in use in the atlas.
stops.campa: He lands at New York on the thirtieth of July expecting a ship and a command, and is offered neither. Antonio Meucci, a Florentine inventor keeping a candle factory at Rosebank on Staten Island, takes him into the house and puts him to dipping tallow. Garibaldi does it for months, shoots in the woods behind the shore, and is by his own account thoroughly wretched. Later Italian memory will make the two men partners in the invention of the telephone. Nothing in the record supports it. He is paid a wage and given a room by a friend.
suggested_refs: Meucci's candle factory and house at 420 Tompkins Avenue, Rosebank, Staten Island

stops.name: Callao, the Carmen and the Pacific
stops.date_confidence: attested for the command of the Carmen and for the sailing of 10 January 1852 reaching Canton in April, by way of Xiamen, Manila, and Three Hummock Island in the Bass Strait. The Peruvian citizenship and the alias Giuseppe Pane used to leave New York are [R].
stops.campa: With Peruvian papers and a merchant master's berth, Garibaldi takes the Carmen out of Callao, loads guano, and then works her west across the Pacific: Canton by April, then Xiamen, Manila, and home the long way about by Three Hummock Island in the Bass Strait. It is a full circuit of the globe, worked rather than travelled, with a cargo manifest at every port. He is forty-five and drawing a master's pay. The Peruvian papers, and the alias he is said to have left New York under, Giuseppe Pane, rest on tradition alone.
suggested_refs: The merchant ship Carmen, sailed from Callao to Canton in 1852

stops.name: Tynemouth, the sword from the Tyne
stops.date_confidence: attested for the arrival on the Tyne aboard the Commonwealth on 21 March 1854, the lodging at Tynemouth, and the presentation of an inscribed sword.
stops.campa: The Commonwealth comes into the Tyne under Garibaldi's command in March and the north-east of England turns out for him. He lodges at Huntingdon Place in Tynemouth, walks the quays at South Shields, and is given an inscribed sword bought by subscription among keelmen, miners, and shipyard workers who have never been nearer Italy than the coal trade. He is a working ship's master, forty-six years old, in a port on the wrong side of Europe. They receive him as a head of state in exile.
suggested_refs: The inscribed sword presented to Garibaldi by subscription on Tyneside, March 1854

stops.name: Caprera, half an island
stops.date_confidence: attested; year corrected. He lands at Genoa on 10 May 1854; the Caprera article dates the purchase of about half the island to 1855 and the acquisition of the northern half to 1856, funded by the inheritance from his brother Felice, who died in 1855. The 1854 purchase date current in the Garibaldi article cannot stand against that. Month and day are placeholders.
stops.campa: He lands at Genoa in May of 1854 with five years of exile behind him. The following year his brother Felice dies and leaves him money, and with it he buys half of Caprera, a granite island off the north-east corner of Sardinia with wind, goats, and no harbour, and buys the northern half the year after that. He lives at first in a hut. Then he builds a low white house in the South American style he learned on the Rio Grande and plants vines and fruit trees. He keeps the island for the rest of his life.
suggested_refs: The Casa Bianca on Caprera, built in the style of a Rio Grande do Sul farmhouse

stops.name: Varese, the volunteers ahead of the armies
stops.date_confidence: attested for the Varese action of 26 May 1859 and for the appointment as major general commanding the Cacciatori delle Alpi.
stops.campa: Cavour, who does not like him and needs him, gives Garibaldi a major general's commission and three thousand volunteers the regular army does not want, the Cacciatori delle Alpi, armed out of the worst muskets in the Sardinian stores. For the first time in his life he holds a commission in a war his own government has declared, and reports to a staff. He takes the volunteers into Lombardy ahead of the armies and beats an Austrian force at Varese on the twenty-sixth of May. The lake country rises behind him as he moves.
suggested_refs: The Cacciatori delle Alpi, volunteer corps of the Second War of Independence

stops.name: San Fermo della Battaglia, above Como
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1859; the day given here follows the standard sequence immediately after Varese and is not independently pinned in the sources consulted.
stops.campa: On the ridge at San Fermo above Como, the day after Varese, the Cacciatori break the Austrians a second time and walk into Como the same night. The whole Alpine lake campaign is fought by volunteers off the flank of the regular war. It works, and Turin notes that the guerrilla of the Rio Grande can hold a corps together for a season inside another man's plan. In July the Peace of Villafranca ends the war with Venice still Austrian. Garibaldi resigns his commission.
suggested_refs: The ridge of San Fermo della Battaglia, above Como

stops.name: Fino Mornasco, a marriage of one morning
stops.date_confidence: attested for the marriage to Giuseppina Raimondi on 24 January 1860 and for his walking out the same day. The coordinate is the commune centroid of Fino Mornasco, not the church itself.
stops.campa: Garibaldi marries Giuseppina Raimondi, eighteen years old, daughter of a marquis who has served under him in the Lombard campaign. He is fifty-two. Immediately after the ceremony a note is handed to him saying the bride is carrying the child of one of his own officers. He asks her whether it is true, is told that it is, and leaves the house that morning. He never lives with her, and the marriage is not annulled for another nineteen years. He is back on Caprera within the month.
suggested_refs: The Raimondi villa at Fino Mornasco, near Como

stops.name: Quarto dei Mille, the rock
stops.date_confidence: attested for the embarkation on the night of 5-6 May 1860. Coordinate corrected to the shore at Quarto dei Mille; the value in general circulation sits about 1.5 km inland, in the hills behind the beach, which will not do for a stop whose whole content is boarding a ship off a rock.
stops.campa: From the rock below the road at Quarto, east of Genoa, roughly a thousand men are put out in small boats to two steamers taken by arrangement from the Rubattino company. Most are from the north and most have never seen Sicily. They carry a mixture of Enfields and old muskets, they have no artillery, and no government has ordered them anywhere. Cavour permits the thing and puts his name to no line of it. Il Piemonte and Il Lombardo clear the gulf before dawn on the sixth with Garibaldi aboard.
suggested_refs: The Scoglio dei Mille at Quarto, and the steamers Il Piemonte and Il Lombardo

stops.name: Marsala, the landing
stops.date_confidence: attested for 11 May 1860. The presence of HMS Argus and HMS Intrepid is attested; the legend that Britain delivered the landing militarily is not supported, and no British gun was fired.
stops.campa: The Thousand come into Marsala at the western tip of Sicily in daylight, into a port where two Royal Navy ships happen to be lying to look after British wine interests. Bourbon vessels stand in and hesitate, unwilling to shell a harbour with the British inside it, and the landing goes ashore substantially unopposed. Not one British gun is fired for Garibaldi. Their presence alone buys him the hour he needs to get a thousand men and their ammunition onto the mole. By evening the column is moving inland.
suggested_refs: The mole at Marsala, and HMS Argus and HMS Intrepid lying in the harbour

stops.name: Salemi, the dictatorship
stops.date_confidence: attested for 14 May 1860 at Salemi. This is the day before Calatafimi, not the day after: the 16 May date in circulation comes from an English phrasing that puts the declaration after the battle, and Italian sources date the dictatorship 14 May to 2 December 1860.
stops.campa: At Salemi, three days after the landing, Garibaldi assumes the dictatorship of Sicily in the name of Victor Emmanuel II, King of Italy, a title Victor Emmanuel does not hold and will not hold for ten months. He has a thousand men, a hill town, and not one battle won. The picciotti, the peasant bands of the interior, begin coming down out of the hills to him. The decree is dated Salemi, the fourteenth of May. The first battle of the expedition is fought the next day.
suggested_refs: The decree of dictatorship issued at Salemi, 14 May 1860

stops.name: Pianto Romano, Calatafimi
stops.date_confidence: attested for 15 May 1860. Coordinate corrected: the battle hill of Pianto Romano lies a few kilometres south-west of Calatafimi-Segesta, not north of the town. Two force counts are in circulation and are not reconciled here: about 3,000 royal troops under Landi in the field against the Thousand plus some 500 insurgents, versus the smaller count of the units actually engaged under Sforza, roughly 1,500 against 800.
stops.campa: On the hill of Pianto Romano outside Calatafimi the Thousand, with about five hundred Sicilian insurgents come in off the countryside, go up a terraced slope at royal troops under General Landi. The royal force in the field numbers some three thousand; the detachment actually engaged, under Sforza, is smaller. Garibaldi walks his line up the terraces in the open, in the red shirt, at fifty-two. They take the hill with the bayonet in the late afternoon. Within a week the whole island is rising.
stops.quote: Qui si fa l'Italia o si muore.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Garibaldi at Calatafimi, 15 May 1860, via Giuseppe Cesare Abba, Storia dei Mille
suggested_refs: The Pianto Romano hill and the Basile ossuary above Calatafimi-Segesta

stops.name: Palermo, street by street
stops.date_confidence: attested for the fighting of 27-30 May 1860, including the Bourbon naval bombardment of the city.
stops.campa: Garibaldi feints inland toward Corleone, sends his guns and his baggage off as a decoy, and comes at Palermo from the south-east through Gibilrossa with the picciotti behind him. The city fights barricade by barricade for three days while the Bourbon fleet shells its own capital from the bay and burns out whole quarters of it. Twenty thousand royal troops holding Palermo open negotiations with a few thousand irregulars, and then embark and sail away. By the first week of June Sicily is his in fact.
suggested_refs: The Gibilrossa approach and the barricades of Palermo, 27-30 May 1860

stops.name: Melito di Porto Salvo, the crossing
stops.date_confidence: attested for the crossing of 19 August 1860 with 3,700 men. Coordinate corrected to the town itself; the value in circulation sits some 4.7 km north-north-west of it, away from the landing beach.
stops.campa: Cavour has written to say the mainland is not to be invaded, and Garibaldi has read the letter. On the night of the nineteenth of August he ferries three thousand seven hundred men across the Strait of Messina and puts them ashore on the Calabrian beach below Melito di Porto Salvo. Reggio falls on the twenty-first. The Bourbon army in Calabria comes apart ahead of him rather than fighting. Towns send their keys out along the road to meet the column. Three weeks take him the length of the peninsula.
suggested_refs: The landing beach below Melito di Porto Salvo, 19 August 1860

stops.name: Naples, entry by train
stops.date_confidence: attested for 7 September 1860. The quote is from the address on delivering flags to the Hungarian hussars, given at Naples in the autumn of 1860 during the dictatorship, printed in full in the Dwight translation of the memoirs; it is placed on this stop as the utterance of the Naples months, not of the day of entry.
stops.campa: Francis II has taken his army out of the city to the Volturno line. Garibaldi comes into Naples ahead of his own troops, by train, with a handful of staff, through streets lined with Bourbon soldiers still under arms and a crowd that will not let the carriage through. He takes possession of the largest city in Italy without a shot fired and against the advice of every man with him. That autumn, handing colours to a squadron of Hungarian hussars in his service, he says what he thinks of the Pope's temporal power.
stops.quote: I am a Christian, and I speak to Christians--I am a good Christian, and speak to good Christians. I love and venerate the religion of Christ, because Christ came into the world to deliver humanity from slavery, for which God has not created it. But the Pope, who wishes all men to be slaves--who demands, of the powerful of the earth, fetters and chains for Italians--the Pope-king does not know Christ: he lies to his religion.
stops.quote_source: Garibaldi's Address on Delivering Flags to the Hungarian Hussars in Naples, autumn 1860, printed in The Life of General Garibaldi, trans. Theodore Dwight (New York: Derby and Jackson, 1861)
suggested_refs: The address to the Hungarian hussars at Naples, autumn 1860
sources: Garibaldi, The Life of General Garibaldi, trans. Dwight, Project Gutenberg 50544, lines 14186-14235

stops.name: The Volturno, near Capua
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1-2 October 1860; the 30 September date in circulation is wrong. The claim that the battle's outcome was decided by the arrival of the Royal Sardinian Army is not supported by the battle article and is not carried here: the Piedmontese regulars arrived afterwards and decided the subsequent siege of Gaeta.
stops.campa: North of Naples on the Volturno the Bourbon army that would not fight for its capital fights for itself: some twenty-five thousand under Ritucci against Garibaldi's thirty thousand, strung out on a line from the sea to Maddaloni. It is the largest battle he ever commands and it takes two days. He rides the line all through the first of them getting his flanks to hold. The royalists fall back on Capua and Gaeta. Piedmontese regulars come up afterwards and take over the sieges.
suggested_refs: The Volturno line from the sea to Maddaloni, 1-2 October 1860

stops.name: Teano, the handing over
stops.date_confidence: attested for the meeting of 26 October 1860. The exact site, the wording, and whether Garibaldi first hailed him as King of Italy are all disputed and heavily ritualised in later iconography.
stops.campa: On the road near Teano Garibaldi rides out to meet Victor Emmanuel II coming south with the regular army, takes off his hat, and hails him King of Italy. Then he hands him the Two Sicilies: nine million people and half the peninsula, taken in five months by volunteers, given away in the open air with no document signed by anybody. He asks for the lieutenancy of the south for one year, and is refused. He asks for nothing else. The King rides on to Naples and Garibaldi rides in the procession behind him.
suggested_refs: The bridge and road at Teano, 26 October 1860, and its later iconography

stops.name: Caprera, the return with nothing
stops.date_confidence: attested for the withdrawal to Caprera on 9 November 1860 and for the refusal of rewards and titles; the specific inventory of what he carried aboard is traditional.
stops.campa: He refuses the princedom, the annual income, the estate, the Order of the Annunziata, and a general's rank in the Sardinian army, and takes ship for Caprera with a sack of seed corn, a bag of coffee, and some dried fish. His volunteers are being disbanded meanwhile without pensions and mostly without rank in the new army, which he does not forgive and never stops writing about. On the island he plants and walks the goat paths. The correspondence arrives by the sackful, from every country in Europe.
suggested_refs: The disbandment of the southern volunteers, 1861, and Garibaldi's refusal of honours

stops.name: Aspromonte, the ten minutes
stops.date_confidence: attested for 29 August 1862, for the two wounds in hip and ankle, for the imprisonment at Varignano near Portovenere, and for the amnesty of 5 October 1862. The extraction of the ball at Pisa by Ferdinando Zannetti on 23 November is attested and belongs to Pisa, not to Varignano.
stops.campa: With two thousand volunteers raised in Sicily under the cry Roma o morte, Garibaldi crosses to Calabria and marches for a Rome the King cannot take and will not permit him to take. Italian regulars intercept him in the pine woods of Aspromonte. He orders his men not to fire on Italians and walks the line saying so; the regulars fire; the whole business lasts ten minutes. Two balls hit him, in the hip and in the ankle. He is carried out and held at the fort of Varignano. Surgeons argue for months over whether the ankle ball is still in there.
suggested_refs: The Forte di Varignano near Porto Venere, and Ferdinando Zannetti's extraction of the ball at Pisa, 23 November 1862

stops.name: Caprera, the letter to Lincoln
stops.date_confidence: attested for the letter of 6 August 1863; the text is excerpted at the American Battlefield Trust from the primary letter.
stops.campa: From the island, still lame, Garibaldi writes to the President of the United States. He had been sounded out for a Union command two years before and had not taken it, wanting the abolition of slavery declared first and a supreme command he was never going to be given. The Emancipation Proclamation has since been issued. He writes now. In the same letter he calls Lincoln the heir of the teaching of Christ and of John Brown. What he would have done with a Union corps is not a question the record answers.
stops.quote: Posterity will call you the great emancipator, a more enviable title than any crown could be
stops.quote_source: Garibaldi, letter to Abraham Lincoln, 6 August 1863
suggested_refs: The Garibaldi letter to Lincoln of 6 August 1863, American Battlefield Trust primary sources

stops.name: Bezzecca, and one word
stops.date_confidence: attested for the battle of 21 July 1866 and for the telegram of 9 August 1866 to General La Marmora. Coordinate corrected to Bezzecca itself in the Val di Ledro; the value in circulation lies some nine kilometres south-east, on the ridge above Lake Garda.
stops.campa: Italy is at war with Austria for Venetia, Garibaldi has the volunteers again, forty thousand of them, and the mountain front in the Trentino. Wounded in the thigh, he directs the fight at Bezzecca in the Val di Ledro from a carriage while his line breaks, holds, and then takes the village. It is the only Italian victory in a war lost at Custoza and lost again at Lissa. Three weeks later, with the road to Trento open in front of him, the order comes to withdraw from the Trentino, and he answers it in one word.
stops.quote_source: Garibaldi, telegram to General Alfonso La Marmora, 9 August 1866
suggested_refs: The Obbedisco telegram of 9 August 1866, and the Val di Ledro front

stops.name: Geneva, the Palais Electoral
stops.date_confidence: attested for the inaugural congress of the League of Peace and Freedom at Geneva on 9 September 1867 and for Garibaldi's presence, this pass by way of mikhail_bakunin.journey.json rather than an independently fetched source.
stops.campa: At the inaugural congress of the League of Peace and Freedom, in a hall that holds John Stuart Mill and Victor Hugo, Garibaldi opens the proceedings. Mikhail Bakunin is in the same hall and takes the floor; he has spent three years building his International Brotherhood among Italian radicals he describes as unemployed since Garibaldi, in the vacuum left when the campaigns stopped short of Rome and Venice. The congress will split within a year over property. Garibaldi is back in Italy inside the month, buying rifles.
suggested_refs: The inaugural congress of the League of Peace and Freedom, Palais Electoral, Geneva, September 1867

stops.name: Mentana, the Chassepots
stops.date_confidence: attested for the occupation of Monterotondo in October 1867 with some 8,100 volunteers, for the battle of 3 November 1867, and for the withdrawal into the Kingdom of Italy the next day with about 5,100 men.
stops.campa: He comes down on Rome a third time, takes Monterotondo in October with some eight thousand volunteers, and waits for the city to rise. It does not rise at the scale the plan requires. At Mentana, papal troops stiffened by a French expeditionary force freshly landed at Civitavecchia meet him with the new Chassepot rifle, which outranges everything his men are carrying by half again. He is stopped in an afternoon. Five thousand one hundred of the eight thousand one hundred cross back into Italian territory the next day.
suggested_refs: The Chassepot rifle at Mentana, 3 November 1867

segments.name: The Last Campaign and the Island

stops.name: Lantenay, the plateau above Dijon
stops.date_confidence: attested for the command of the Army of the Vosges and for the Lantenay ambush, which belongs to November 1870, before the Dijon fighting of January 1871; the two are often merged into a single span and are kept apart here. Coordinate corrected to the commune of Lantenay, Cote-d'Or; the day is a placeholder.
stops.campa: France is a republic again and at war, and Garibaldi, who has spent thirty years fighting French armies in Italy, offers it whatever is left of him. He is sixty-three, arthritic, and cannot get on a horse unaided. The Army of the Vosges he is handed is fifteen thousand irregulars of every nationality in Europe, and in November he ambushes advancing Prussian columns from the plateau above Dijon at Lantenay. The fighting for Dijon itself comes in January, and his volunteers hold the city longer than any other French force holds anything that winter.
suggested_refs: The Army of the Vosges, and the plateau of Lantenay above Dijon

stops.name: Bordeaux, the Assembly shouts him down
stops.date_confidence: attested for the February 1871 session at Bordeaux, for Hugo being shouted down over Garibaldi's eligibility, and for Hugo's resignation days afterwards; the exact sitting day is not pinned in the sources consulted. Coordinate inherited from the Bordeaux pin already in use in the atlas.
stops.campa: Elected to the National Assembly by four departments at once, Garibaldi comes to Bordeaux to take a seat, and the monarchist majority of a beaten France will not hear a foreigner speak in it. Victor Hugo rises to defend his eligibility and is shouted down; Hugo resigns his own seat within days, and buries his son Charles in the same week. Garibaldi has already put his resignation on the president's desk and gone out of the hall. He never sets foot in France again.
suggested_refs: The February 1871 session of the French National Assembly at Bordeaux

stops.name: Caprera, the marriage to Francesca Armosino
stops.date_confidence: attested for the marriage in 1880 to Francesca Armosino, with whom he already had children; the day given follows the annulment of the 1860 marriage in January of that year and is not independently pinned. The publication dates of the novels are attested.
stops.campa: Francesca Armosino came to Caprera as a nurse to a grandchild and has stayed. Three of their children have been born on the island. The marriage of one morning in 1860 is annulled at last, and Garibaldi marries her, seventy-two years old, in a wheelchair on most days, farming an island he can no longer walk across and writing novels to pay for the farming: Cantoni il volontario in 1870, The Rule of the Monk in the same year, I Mille in 1874. He has sat in the Chamber of Deputies almost continuously since February 1861.
suggested_refs: Cantoni il volontario (1870), The Rule of the Monk (1870), and I Mille (1874)

stops.name: Caprera, the clock at 6:21
stops.date_confidence: attested for the death at Caprera on 2 June 1882 at 6:21 pm, for the testament asking cremation and part burial under a juniper, and for the request not being carried out. The spring journey to Naples and Palermo for the sixth centenary of the Sicilian Vespers is attested.
stops.campa: He dies at twenty-one minutes past six in the evening, seventy-four years old, in the low white house on the island he bought with a dead brother's money, having gone that spring to Naples and Palermo for the sixth centenary of the Sicilian Vespers and never got his strength back after the journey. His will asks for cremation, and for part of the ash to lie under a juniper. It is not done. He is embalmed and put in a rough granite grave a few steps behind the house. The clock in the room is left stopped at the hour.
suggested_refs: The granite grave behind the Casa Bianca, and the Compendio Garibaldino at Caprera, where the clock and calendar in the death room remain set to 2 June 1882
